guide.title: Stuyvesant Heights, Brooklyn: 577 Landmarked Rowhouses Inside Bed-Stuy
guide.intro: Stuyvesant Heights supplies the second half of Bedford-Stuyvesant's name, and it sits inside the larger neighborhood rather than beside it: New York City Planning's current Neighborhood Tabulation Area scheme has no polygon called Stuyvesant Heights at all, folding the area into Bedford-Stuyvesant (East), code BK0302, in Brooklyn Community District 3. What sets it apart is a landmark district rather than a city boundary. The area takes its name from Stuyvesant Avenue, its principal thoroughfare, itself named for Peter Stuyvesant, the last Director-General of the Dutch colony of New Netherland; for most of its early history it was outlying farmland belonging to the older settlement of Bedford. The first row of masonry houses went up in 1872 on MacDonough Street for the developer Curtis L. North.

sections.heading: A district, not a boundary
sections.body:
Most of the neighborhood's rowhouses and apartment buildings with ground-floor storefronts were built between about 1870 and 1920, with development accelerating sharply between 1895 and 1900.

The Stuyvesant Heights Historic District covers 577 contributing residential buildings from roughly 1870 to 1900, mostly two- and three-story high-basement rowhouses in Italianate, Second Empire and Queen Anne Revival styles, on streets including MacDonough, Decatur, Chauncey, Lewis and Stuyvesant. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on December 4, 1975, with the listed boundary expanded on November 15, 1996. The New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission designated an Expanded Stuyvesant Heights Historic District on April 16, 2013, extending the locally landmarked area north to Jefferson Avenue, east to Malcolm X Boulevard and west to Tompkins Avenue.

Three churches stand within the district and are named as its landmarks: Our Lady of Victory Catholic Church, Mount Lebanon Baptist Church and St. Phillip's Episcopal Church. Our Lady of Victory's parish was established in 1868, and its church of dark Manhattan schist trimmed in white limestone, at Throop Avenue and MacDonough Street, was built between 1891 and 1895 to designs by the architect Thomas F. Houghton.

Herbert Von King Park lies immediately west. Its eastern edge runs along Tompkins Avenue, the same street the Landmarks Preservation Commission uses as the historic district's western boundary, so sources describe the park as being in Bedford-Stuyvesant generally rather than in Stuyvesant Heights.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
No subway station is recorded as sitting inside Stuyvesant Heights itself, so the useful stations are the Bedford-Stuyvesant ones on either side of it, and the buses that run along the historic district's boundary streets.

The IND Fulton Street Line runs beneath Fulton Street, the historic district's southern boundary street. Utica Avenue, at Utica Avenue and Fulton Street in Bedford-Stuyvesant, is served by the A at all times, express by day and local late nights, and by the C at all times except late nights. Kingston-Throop Avenues, on Fulton Street between Kingston and Throop Avenues in Bedford-Stuyvesant, and Ralph Avenue, at Ralph Avenue and Fulton Street, are each served by the C at all times except late nights and the A late nights only; the Ralph Avenue source names both Bedford-Stuyvesant and Ocean Hill.

On the elevated BMT Jamaica Line to the north, Halsey Street is served by the J at all times, and Gates Avenue and Chauncey Street each by the J at all times except peak-direction rush hours and the Z during peak-direction rush hours only. Sources place Halsey Street and Gates Avenue at the border of Bedford-Stuyvesant and Bushwick, and Chauncey Street in Bedford-Stuyvesant and Bushwick; none of the three is assigned to Stuyvesant Heights.

Buses reach the district more directly. The B25 runs mainly along Fulton Street, the historic district's southern boundary street, stopping at Tompkins, Lewis and Stuyvesant Avenues. The B46, local and Select Bus Service, runs along Malcolm X Boulevard, the district's eastern boundary street. The B15 runs south from Woodhull Medical Center on Marcus Garvey Boulevard southbound and Lewis Avenue northbound, and Lewis Avenue runs through the district's interior. The B26 reaches Halsey Street by way of Fulton Street, Putnam Avenue and the Nostrand and Bedford Avenue corridor.

faq.question: How do I get to Stuyvesant Heights?
faq.answer: The nearest subway stations are Bedford-Stuyvesant's. Utica Avenue on the A and C, and Kingston-Throop Avenues and Ralph Avenue on the C, with the A late nights, all sit on Fulton Street, which forms the historic district's southern edge. Halsey Street on the J, and Gates Avenue and Chauncey Street on the J and Z, sit on the Jamaica Line to the north. The B25 along Fulton Street and the B46 along Malcolm X Boulevard run on the district's own boundary streets.

faq.question: Is Stuyvesant Heights part of Bedford-Stuyvesant?
faq.answer: It sits inside it. New York City Planning's current Neighborhood Tabulation Area scheme has no polygon named Stuyvesant Heights; the area is folded into Bedford-Stuyvesant (East), code BK0302, in Brooklyn Community District 3. The name survives through the landmark district rather than through any official city boundary.

faq.question: Where can I stay in Stuyvesant Heights?
faq.answer: Akwaaba Mansion, a four-room bed-and-breakfast in a restored 1860s Italianate villa at 347 MacDonough Street. Its operator describes the property as being in the historic Stuyvesant Heights neighborhood and states that it marked 30 years in business as of 2025.

places.name: Stuyvesant Heights Historic District
places.address: Roughly bounded by Tompkins Avenue, Jefferson Avenue, Malcolm X Boulevard and Fulton Street, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: 577 contributing rowhouses and apartment buildings, built roughly 1870 to 1900 in Italianate, Second Empire and Queen Anne Revival styles, most of them two- and three-story houses with high basements. Not a single site but a walkable streetscape, with the densest blocks on MacDonough, Decatur, Chauncey, Lewis and Stuyvesant.
places.history: The district was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on December 4, 1975, and the listed boundary was expanded on November 15, 1996. The New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission designated an Expanded Stuyvesant Heights Historic District on April 16, 2013, extending the locally landmarked area north to Jefferson Avenue, east to Malcolm X Boulevard and west to Tompkins Avenue.

places.name: Our Lady of Victory Church
places.address: Throop Avenue and MacDonough Street, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: A church of dark Manhattan schist trimmed in white limestone, built between 1891 and 1895 to designs by the architect Thomas F. Houghton, and named as one of the Stuyvesant Heights Historic District's landmarks.
places.history: The parish was established in 1868. In 2011 the Diocese of Brooklyn consolidated it with two others to form St. Martin de Porres Parish, which continues to use the building for worship.

places.name: Chez Oskar
places.summary: A French restaurant on Decatur Street, an interior street of the historic district. City health department inspection records list the restaurant at this address through its most recent inspection, on April 14, 2026, with a Grade A.

places.name: Akwaaba Mansion
places.summary: A restored 1860s Italianate villa run as a four-room bed-and-breakfast, furnished with Afrocentric decor and antiques, with a garden and a ballroom holding a baby grand piano. The operator describes the property as being in the historic Stuyvesant Heights neighborhood and states that it marked 30 years in business as of 2025.
places.history: The house stands on MacDonough Street, the same street where the first row of masonry houses in Stuyvesant Heights was built in 1872 for the developer Curtis L. North.
